entries.name: Particle swarm optimization
entries.definition: A population-based optimization method that moves candidate particles through a search space using retained velocities and stochastic attraction toward remembered personal and shared best positions.
entries.identity_notes: The record describes continuous particle swarm optimization through the inspected global-best formulation. The 1995 simplified update retains the old velocity with coefficient 1 and uses two attraction coefficients equal to 2; the later inertia-weighted formulation is an explicit variant. It is not differential evolution, an objective-gradient method, a biological flock simulation, a trained neural network or an exact description of every discrete, neighborhood or constricted PSO variant. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: Current positions can overshoot remembered bests and have worse objective values. Attraction to a best-so-far position is not attraction to a known global optimum. If every particle has zero velocity and its current position equals both remembered attractors, this displayed rule has no motion; the fixed state need not be optimal.

The original coefficient 1 on old velocity and the later inertia weight must not be conflated. The 1999 experiment’s decreasing weight and Vmax/Xmax settings are particular choices, not universal optimal settings or a complete bound-repair specification. Clipping a velocity alone does not ensure a feasible position.

The full random-stream coupling, synchronous versus asynchronous best updates, ties, constraints and noisy evaluations require declared implementation choices. The social analogy is not a convergence proof. The 1999 discussion explicitly allows failure to find the required optimum; no universal speed, accuracy or finite-budget global-optimum guarantee is asserted.

claims.statement: Initialize a population of real-valued positions and velocities and evaluate the objective. Retain each particle’s best evaluated position and the best position shared across the population. For each coordinate in the inspected global-best rule, add two randomly scaled displacements to the retained velocity: one from the current position toward the personal best and one toward the global best. The baseline is v_new=v+c1*r1*(p−x)+c2*r2*(g−x), followed by x_new=x+v_new; the source gives random factors in [0,1]. Evaluate the resulting positions and refresh the remembered bests when improved. Particles remain population members rather than undergoing target-trial survival selection. In the 1995 simplified version c1=c2=2. The 1999 inertia variant replaces the retained term v by w*v and studies a decreasing w schedule. Initialization, population size, coefficients, velocity limits, boundary treatment, update ordering and stopping rules must be specified for an executable configuration.

entries.name: Simulated annealing
entries.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The later mathematical conditions for asymptotic annealing convergence were not audited here. No electronic-design or traveling-salesman benchmark is reproduced.

claims.statement: Choose a representation of feasible configurations, an objective E to minimize, a random rearrangement proposal and an annealing schedule specifying temperatures and work at each temperature. At current configuration x, propose y and compute delta=E(y)−E(x). For the basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis rule at effective temperature T>0 measured in cost units, accept delta<=0 moves and accept delta>0 with probability exp(−delta/T); otherwise retain x. Repeat transitions at the current temperature, then lower temperature according to the schedule. High temperatures permit larger cost-increasing moves more frequently; cooling reduces that probability. The source motivates sufficient equilibration at each stage. Candidate representation, move set and schedule depend on the optimization problem; the returned low-cost configuration is a search result rather than a certified global minimizer.

entries.name: Cross-entropy optimization
entries.definition: A stochastic optimization method that iteratively samples a parameterized search distribution, selects high-performing samples using an adaptive threshold, and refits the distribution by maximum likelihood on those selected samples.
entries.identity_notes: This is the optimization branch of the cross-entropy method, represented by Algorithm2.3 in the inspected 2005 tutorial. It is distinct from the rare-event probability estimator, the cross-entropy loss used to train a classifier, NES natural-gradient steps, and CMA-ES evolution-path covariance adaptation. The sampling family and its fit define concrete instances; the generic algorithm is not limited to independent Bernoulli variables or a Gaussian implementation. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: A score>=threshold rule need not select exactly rho*N candidates: order-statistic indexing and tied scores can increase the elite count. Implementations must state their quantile, tie and optimization-direction conventions; minimization requires the corresponding lower-score criterion or an equivalent score transformation.

Unsmoothed finite-sample fitting can produce Bernoulli probabilities 0 or 1 and remove future exploration. Interior initialization and 0<alpha<1 prevent exact endpoints after a single convex smoothing step in exact arithmetic; smoothing alone does not guarantee exploration forever or a global optimum, and finite precision can still collapse support.

The choice of sampling family, initial support, sample size, elite fraction, fit constraints and stopping rule matters. A stabilized threshold is not an optimality certificate; the source explicitly permits getting trapped at a local minimum and limits its asymptotic discussion.

Maximum-likelihood fitting of selected candidates is a sampling-distribution update, not an unbiased gradient of raw expected fitness. It does not require derivatives of the black-box objective; solving the distribution fit may still require numerical optimization. No universal performance or convergence-rate claim is curated.

definition_evidence.locator: Section2.2, Algorithm2.3 and Remarks2.3–2.6, PDF pp.15–19 / printed33–37; Equation20, PDFp.12 / printed30; KL direction in Section2.1, PDF pp.10–11; discussion PDFp.46 / printed64

claims.statement: Specify a sampling family f(x;v), initial parameter, sample size N, elite parameter rho and stopping rule. For maximization, draw candidates from the current distribution, evaluate their scores and choose the empirical (1−rho) quantile as threshold gamma. Fit new parameters by maximizing the sum of log f(x;v) over sampled candidates with score at least gamma. The optimization formulation uses unit weights: it redefines the associated stochastic problem at each iteration, so the rare-event algorithm’s nominal-to-current likelihood ratio is absent. Optionally smooth the fitted parameter toward the old one via v_new=alpha*v_fit+(1−alpha)*v_old. For independent Bernoulli coordinates, the unsmoothed fit is the coordinatewise fraction of ones among selected samples. Iterate until the chosen stopping condition; the displayed Algorithm2.3 uses an unchanged threshold over several iterations. The source’s cross-entropy derivation minimizes KL from the ideal selected-event distribution to the parameterized sampling distribution, not the reverse direction.

native_neighbors.name: Differential Evolution
native_neighbors.definition: A population-based continuous optimization method that generates trial vectors using scaled differences between population members, combines mutant and target coordinates, and selects replacements through target-trial objective comparisons.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes differential evolution, with the 1997 DE/rand/1/bin procedure as its explicitly inspected core. Mutation/crossover variants are distinguished by the source’s DE/x/y/z notation rather than treated as identical executable rules. It differs from generic genetic algorithms, a fitted Gaussian search distribution, objective-gradient descent, and DEHB’s additional budget-specific populations and Hyperband scheduling. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 270 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 19 and 19 lines respectively. These were prior candidate leads, source discussions and neighboring DEHB/FABOLAS method mentions. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The prose specifies replacement for a strictly smaller objective, whereas the displayed C-style Figure3 uses <=. The tie policy must therefore be identified when implementing or comparing versions; these source statements are not treated as identical code. A forced mutant coordinate need not change its numerical value.

DE/rand/1/bin needs at least four population members for its distinct-index rule. Difference-vector proposals can leave the initialization range; that range is not a hard feasible-domain boundary. Bound repair, general constraint handling, noise treatment and categorical encodings are additional choices.

The method uses function evaluations, not derivatives of the objective. Population collapse can eliminate difference-vector variation, and finite-budget greedy selection does not certify a global optimum. The source’s control-variable suggestions and comparative results are empirical, not universal guarantees or reproduced experiments.

claims.statement: Maintain a fixed-size population of real-valued vectors. In the inspected DE/rand/1/bin scheme, for each target select three mutually distinct current-generation population indices that also differ from the target index. Add a scaled difference of two selected vectors to the third to form a mutant. Build a trial by independently choosing mutant or target coordinates according to the crossover probability, forcing one randomly selected coordinate to come from the mutant. Evaluate the trial and use a greedy comparison against its target to choose the next-generation member. Complete all target comparisons using the old population before replacing it with the next population. Repeat until the configured stopping criterion is met. Population size, mutation scale, crossover probability and initialization are configuration choices.

native_neighbors.name: Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy
native_neighbors.definition: An evolution strategy for continuous optimization that samples a multivariate normal search distribution and adapts its mean, covariance and global step size from ranked offspring and accumulated selected-step paths.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record describes CMA-ES through the 2001 weighted-recombination algorithm and its author-supplied errata. That algorithm’s covariance update is based on a rank-one evolution-path outer product; later rank-mu, active covariance, restart and limited-memory variants are not silently imported. The search distribution is not a predictive model of objective values. Derandomized adaptation does not make offspring sampling deterministic. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 270 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 19 and 19 lines respectively. These were prior candidate leads, source discussions and neighboring DEHB/FABOLAS method mentions. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: This is a source-specific account of the 2001 algorithm, not an exact implementation contract for all contemporary CMA-ES software. Its positive recombination weights, rank-one covariance update and cumulative step-size rule are distinguished from later extensions. The author errata qualify the default weight formula when the selected-parent count exceeds half the offspring population and revise a suggested ordering of cumulation parameters.

Initial mean and step size matter. Weak, noisy or selection-irrelevant feedback and numerical conditioning can impair covariance adaptation or collapse short search directions. Full covariance storage grows quadratically with dimension; eigendecomposition and expensive function evaluations add computational costs.

Constraint handling and termination require explicit choices. The paper discusses resampling feasible offspring but cautions about boundary optima. Ranking and distribution adaptation do not guarantee a global optimum, monotonic improvement of every generation, or a calibrated inverse-Hessian estimate. native_neighbors.name: Metropolis–Hastings sampling
native_neighbors.definition: A Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that proposes a new state from a specified transition distribution and accepts it with the smaller of one and the target-density ratio multiplied by the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio, otherwise retaining the current state.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the usual Metropolis acceptance choice within Hastings’s more general family of reversible updates. It is not the whole MCMC family, a Markov-chain model, the Barker acceptance rule or an independent-draw generator. Asymmetric proposals require the proposal-ratio correction. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 153 prior native IDs/names/aliases. Both checkout text searches included ignored and hidden files and returned no matches for the selected exact IDs, full labels, aliases and source titles. Existing HMM and Markov random field records describe probability models, not these sampling or tuning procedures.
limitations: The target must be proper, and the proposal and acceptance calculation must be defined on the relevant support. A proposed move with no reverse support has zero acceptance; zero-over-zero expressions are not a general operational rule.
Target invariance does not ensure irreducibility, aperiodicity, rapid mixing, independent samples or convergence from every start. Those properties depend on the target and proposal.
Rejections repeat the current state. Keeping only accepted moves without correcting their weighting changes the sampling process.
Poor proposals, isolated modes, finite precision and inadequate run length can yield misleading estimates; acceptance rate alone does not establish adequate exploration.
The record does not reproduce an implementation or assert a universal acceptance target, speed improvement or numerical posterior result.
